newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Ex-HK to Europe airlines plan cargo rate rises.
newsitem.headline: Ex-HK to Europe airlines plan cargo rate rises.

text.p: Cargo managers of major airlines from Hong Kong to European destinations have agreed to raise air cargo rates by HK$3 per kilo from August 1. They also plan another HK$3 per kilo rise when their winter schedules begin on October 1, industry sources told Reuters.
The moves come with the air cargo market between the territory and Europe awaiting the end of its traditional slack season as Hong Kong counts down the final days to the end of colonial rule.

Most rates from Hong Kong to major European destinations such as London and Frankfurt are currently reported to vary between HK$19-23 per kilo depending on the level of service and the carrier involved.
Among airlines expected to raise ex Hong Kong rates are Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd, Air France, Lufthansa Cargo, China Airlines Korean Airlines Ltd, Malaysian Airlines and Singapore Airlines.

Airline managers said they were determined to increase yield and, after a good first half, were confident of being able to take advantage of an anticipated strong peak season by pressing through the further rises.

British Airways Plc said it had already decided to raise ex Hong Kong rates to the UK by HK$3 per kilo from August 1. The British carrier, which operates three weekly freighters to London Stansted supplementing belly cargo space aboard 15 Boeing 747-400 passenger flights, said it would also consider another HK$3 per kilo rate rise from October 1.

"It is up to individual airlines to put up their rates but we had our rate rise planned for some time. We are confident that August is the right time for a rise when we expect the market to be strong. I don't see any reason why our competitors will not do the same," Chris Chan, BA World Cargo's Greater China area manager, said.
Freight forwarders reacted with alarm when told about the proposed twin rate increases.
"Two rate rises will kill the market," said one shocked freight forwarder.
"It puts us in a difficult position if they raise rates because we will have to absorb a large part of the rise and we can't pass it on to customers. Our profit margin will suffer," he added.
Freight forwarders generally described the European market as living up to its traditional slack season pattern and is now weak.
"There is not enough cargo to fill up space," said Burton Chan of LEP Far East Ltd which specialises in shipping high value computer equipment.
He said the Hong Kong air freight market is being increasingly affected by rising levels of cargo being airfreighted directly to Europe from Chinese airports such as Beijing, Shanghai and Guangzhou.
"I think in the coming years the situation will become more serious (for Hong Kong). It is also much cheaper to airfreight out of China so Hong Kong is becoming less competitive," Chan said.
"The market to Europe is not exciting at all," said Thomas Miu, general manager of the air freight division of Jardine Freight Services and part of the Jardine Matheson Group.
Freight forwarders agreed that traffic levels to London were much higher than to Hong Kong's traditional leading European cargo destination, Frankfurt.
"The UK is much the stronger market at the moment both for in bound and outbound cargo," said forwarder Thomas Miu.
Lufthansa Cargo said the handover has had no effect on business.
"Nothing has changed and it has been a case of business as usual with no rise in demand over the handover," according to one Lufthansa executive.

The political and economic situation in Germany is not helping trade and loads have been average or a little below, according to the carrier's China, Hong Kong and Taiwan managing director, Christian Sedelmaier.

But the German carrier, which ranks Hong Kong number five in its worldwide network for tonnage and Hong Kong and China traffic also accounts for 24 per cent of total business in Asia, anticipates an increase in demand to begin from the middle of July onwards as the peak season begins.
Lufthansa is optimistic for both the near and long term future and is planning to add extra capacity.

Sedelmaier said the Hong Kong to Frankfurt B747 freighter service, which is operated in conjunction with partners Cathay Pacific Cargo, is expected to increase to 12 flights per week later this year and become twice daily within two years.

Lufthansa's partner, Cathay Pacific Cargo, was more positive about the recent level of business and reported a strong market for freighter traffic to Europe with an increase in load factors over last year's levels.

"June is looking very good and ex-Europe is looking good as well with Frankfurt reporting substantial double digit growth out of Europe as well. Things are looking pretty good for us," said Ray Jewell, Cathay Cargo's sales and marketing manager.
With the peak season on the horizon, Jewell said he was looking toward raising yield with rate rise.

Forwarding firms said the handover had definitely affected the level of business at Kai Tak recently as factories in southern China cleared their factory floors before their workers went on holiday and Hong Kong began its five day official holiday.
But the rush to clear goods has not been as frantic to European destinations as to U.S airports due to over-capacity on west bound routes out of Hong Kong.
Forwarders said although deals were being done, rates had generally dropped by 10 to 15 percent over the last month as capacity exceeded demand.
"During May and June the market has been soft so we've see a fall in rates of one or two dollars per kilo," said one large forwarder's spokesman.
Emirates Airline, which flies from Hong Kong to London via its Dubai hub, described the current market as "quite slow".
Emirates cargo manager in Hong Kong, Jacky Lau, said seasonal demand was greater for ex-Dubai flights to the UK than from Hong Kong and some Airbus A310 flights to the Middle East had been light.
Lau also hoped the market would pick up as soon as the middle of July.
Typical selling rates for Dubai were around HK$16-17 per kg with rates to Europe quoted by sources as being between HK$19-22 kg.

Virgin Atlantic Airways operates daily Airbus A340 passenger flights, reported a busy month for cargo to London with increased loads possible because more passengers were flying to Hong Kong for the handover than were leaving, allowing maximum cargo loads. For instance, students, a key passenger market for Virgin, were one group staying in the territory until after the handover.

A cargo spokesman also said rates had gradually risen during June by between HK$1-2 and was forecasting July to be a busy month. Virgin is also expecting to raise its rates along with other carriers to Europe from August 1.
One cargo source pointed out that if the market accepts two rates rises of HK$3 each, that would restore some rates close to HK$30 per kilo "and the good old days of a few years ago."

"But for all airlines to maintain a set rate is always a questionable business. Someone usually breaks ranks and does deals to fill space. I don't know whether the market will stand for it" the source added.
BA said recent cargo demand had been much better than expected after fears that the Chinese border would close to freight traffic before the handover failed to materialise.
Like many carriers, BA was unsure of what the demand for cargo space would be over the handover period but was pleased with the level of business leading up to the historic day.

BA said it had reshuffled its schedules during the handover but because demand for inbound services was still present there would be no cancellations. A major proportion of outbound space would be reallocated to Delhi in India where the freighters stop on the way back to the UK.
BA also said its recent move for Hong Kong cargo to Stansted from Gatwick had gone smoothly and customers were happy with what it described as increased levels of service.
Over the handover period, BA is arranging three extra passenger flights to carry British troops and civilians back to the UK as well as a special royal flight hours after the handover ceremonies.

BA is another carrier considering increasing Hong Kong-UK capacity. It currently operates a Boeing 747-200 freighter with 100 tonnes capacity three times weekly between Hong Kong and London Stansted via Delhi and Bahrain.
Chan said he hopes the service will become five times weekly sometime in the autumn. BA already has the necessary traffic rights under the bilateral air agreement between the UK and China.

Aviation analysts said there has been a general increase in cargo capacity over the past nine months since European airlines such as BA, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines and Virgin Atlantic were allowed to use a new shorter route over central China to Europe which cut up to 90 minutes off flight times.

The reduced fuel load needed meant extra cargo capacity could be carried and this was being reflected in recent statistics with big increases in RTKs for instance recorded by Cathay Pacific, analysts said.

The question of when the current slack season market will be revived with the start of the peak season received mixed responses. The peak season to the USA may begin as early as the middle of July, but some forwarders said the peak season to Europe is not expected to begin until August or the start of September.

The more bullish view came from airlines such as Lufthansa and British Airways which said they expect the peak season to begin as early as the middle of July - followed by the rate rises forwarders are dreading. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
